notes.front: What are an aeroplane's position lights?
notes.back: Coloured lights on the wingtips and tail, arranged like those of boats and ships.
notes.explanation: The arrangement lets a pilot judge the general direction of movement of other aeroplanes in flight.
notes.example: Like the coloured sidelights a ship shows at night, but mounted on an aeroplane's wingtips and tail.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airplane Equipment and Lighting”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Airplane position lights are arranged similar to those of boats and ships. A red light is positioned on the left wingtip, a green light on the right wingtip, and a white light on the tail. [Figure 11-4]

notes.front: What is a black-hole approach?
notes.back: A night landing made over water or unlit terrain, where the runway lights are the only source of light.
notes.explanation: Without peripheral visual cues to help, orientation is difficult.
notes.example: Like driving towards a single lit doorway across a dark field, but you must judge a descent to it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Featureless Terrain Illusion”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: A black-hole approach occurs when the landing is made from over water or non-lighted terrain where the runway lights are the only source of light. Without peripheral visual cues to help, orientation is difficult.

notes.front: Which wingtip carries the red position light?
notes.back: The left wingtip.
notes.explanation: The layout follows boats and ships: red left, green right, white on the tail.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airplane Equipment and Lighting”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Airplane position lights are arranged similar to those of boats and ships. A red light is positioned on the left wingtip, a green light on the right wingtip, and a white light on the tail.

notes.front: What colour is the position light on the right wingtip?
notes.back: Green.
notes.explanation: The red light is on the left wingtip and the white light on the tail.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airplane Equipment and Lighting”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Airplane position lights are arranged similar to those of boats and ships. A red light is positioned on the left wingtip, a green light on the right wingtip, and a white light on the tail.

notes.front: Where is the white position light?
notes.back: On the tail.
notes.explanation: The two wingtips carry the coloured lights: red on the left, green on the right.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airplane Equipment and Lighting”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Airplane position lights are arranged similar to those of boats and ships. A red light is positioned on the left wingtip, a green light on the right wingtip, and a white light on the tail.

notes.front: Without supplemental oxygen, above what altitude can night flight cause hypoxia that impairs vision?
notes.back: Above 5,000 feet at night (against 10,000 feet by day).
notes.explanation: Hypoxia from low barometric pressure impairs visual performance, and the handbook sets a lower threshold at night.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Factors Affecting Vision”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Inflight exposure to low barometric pressure without the use of supplemental oxygen (above 10,000 feet during the day and above 5,000 feet at night) can result in hypoxia, which impairs visual performance.

notes.front: Dark-adapted eyes are exposed to a bright light, such as a landing light, for 1 second or more. What happens?
notes.back: Night vision is temporarily impaired.
notes.explanation: Anti-collision light flashes last under a second, so they do not impair dark adaptation.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Vision Under Dim and Bright Illumination”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Exposure to aircraft anti-collision lights does not impair night vision adaptation because the intermittent flashes have a very short duration (less than 1 second). However, if dark-adapted eyes are exposed to a bright light source (searchlights, landing lights, flares, etc.) for a period of 1 second or more, night vision is temporarily impaired.

notes.front: Why use red flight deck lighting only where the best outside night vision is needed?
notes.back: Red light distorts chart colours: magenta and yellow look red, and cyan looks black.
notes.explanation: Dim white flight deck lighting should be available for reading maps and instruments.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Factors Affecting Vision”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Red light illumination distorts colors (magenta and yellow pigments both appear as red, and cyan pigment appears black) on aeronautical charts. Pilots should use it only where optimum outside night vision capability is necessary. Dim white flight deck lighting should be available when needed for map and instrument reading.

notes.front: With a white/red flashlight at night, what is each light used for?
notes.back: White: the preflight inspection. Red: flight deck operations. Dim white: chart reading.
notes.explanation: Charts shown on an EFB need no flashlight at all.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Pilot Equipment”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: The white light is used while performing the preflight visual inspection of the airplane, the red light is used when performing flight deck operations, and the dim white light may be used for chart reading. Many charts can be displayed on a EFB, which does not require a flashlight.

notes.front: On night cross-country charts, course lines should be drawn in {{c1::black}}.
notes.explanation: Black lines are more distinguishable in low-light conditions.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Preparation and Preflight”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: On night cross-country flights, pilots should select and use appropriate aeronautical charts to include the appropriate adjacent charts. Course lines should be drawn in black to be more distinguishable in low-light conditions.

notes.front: At some airports, what colour are the runway threshold lights?
notes.back: Aviation green.
notes.explanation: Straight lines of lights across the runway ends mark its length limits.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airport and Navigation Lighting Aids”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: The length limits of the runway are defined by straight lines of lights across the runway ends. At some airports, the runway threshold lights are aviation green, and the runway end lights are aviation red.

notes.front: At some airports, what colour are the runway end lights?
notes.back: Aviation red.
notes.explanation: The threshold lights at the same airports are aviation green; together the lines across each end mark the runway's length.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airport and Navigation Lighting Aids”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: The length limits of the runway are defined by straight lines of lights across the runway ends. At some airports, the runway threshold lights are aviation green, and the runway end lights are aviation red.

notes.front: What is the worst-case result of a black-hole approach?
notes.back: Landing short of the runway.
notes.explanation: The runway can seem out of position, sloping down or up.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Featureless Terrain Illusion”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: The runway can seem out of position (down-sloping or up-sloping) and in the worst case, results in landing short of the runway.

notes.front: At night, a runway has a city in the distance on higher terrain beyond it. Which way will you tend to err on the approach?
notes.back: Towards a lower-than-normal approach.
notes.explanation: Reviewing the airfield layout and boundaries before the approach helps keep a safe approach angle.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Featureless Terrain Illusion”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If the runway has a city in the distance on higher terrain, the tendency is to fly a lower-than-normal approach. A good review of the airfield layout and boundaries before initiating any approach helps maintain a safe approach angle.

notes.front: Bright runway and approach lights with few lights around them make the runway seem closer. Which way will you tend to err?
notes.back: Towards a higher approach.
notes.explanation: The bright lighting creates the illusion of being lower, or of having less distance to the runway.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Featureless Terrain Illusion”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Bright runway and approach lighting systems, especially where few lights illuminate the surrounding terrain, may create the illusion of being lower or having less distance to the runway. In this situation, the tendency is to fly a higher approach.

notes.front: What are two physical reactions that continuous flickering light at about 1 to 20 hertz can, rarely, cause?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: nausea, dizziness, confusion.
notes.explanation: The handbook advises eliminating or screening out any light source that might cause such a reaction.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Factors Affecting Vision”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Although rare, this may occur at a frequencies from 1 to 20 hertz. If continuous, the possible physical reactions can be nausea, dizziness, grogginess, unconsciousness, headaches, or confusion. Pilots should try to eliminate or screen out any light source that might cause an unwanted reaction to blinking or flickering lights.

notes.front: Landing at night with landing lights, what cue helps identify when to begin the round out?
notes.back: The landing lights reflecting on the runway and tyre marks becoming clearly visible.
notes.explanation: Inexperienced pilots tend to round out too high at night; the reflected lights and tyre marks help identify the point.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Approaches and Landings”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: An inexperienced pilot may have a tendency to round out too high. Continuing a constant approach descent until the landing lights reflect on the runway and tire marks on the runway can be seen clearly helps identify the point to begin the round out.

notes.front: Landing without landing lights, what cue may start the round out?
notes.back: The runway lights at the far end first appearing to rise higher than the nose.
notes.explanation: This demands a smooth and very timely round out.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Approaches and Landings”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: During landings without the use of landing lights, the round out may be started when the runway lights at the far end of the runway first appear to be rising higher than the nose of the airplane. This demands a smooth and very timely round out

notes.front: How does the 'night' of the night passenger-currency rule differ from the period when position lights must be on?
notes.back: Currency: 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. Position lights: from sunset to sunrise.
notes.explanation: So landings soon after sunset need lights on but do not count toward night passenger currency.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: no person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, unless within the preceding 90 days that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Sunset is at 19:10. At 19:20, while it is still quite light, you start to taxi for a flight. Must your position lights be on?
notes.back: A) Yes: lighted position lights are required from sunset to sunrise
notes.explanation: The rule begins at sunset itself, not when it gets dark or at the end of civil twilight; only Alaska has a different test.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: lighted position lights are required from sunset to sunrise
B) No: only from the end of evening civil twilight
C) No: only from 1 hour after sunset
notes.choicesExplained: B: civil twilight defines night in § 1.1, not the lighting rule. C: 1 hour after sunset is the passenger-currency period.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.209 Aircraft lights (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: During the period from sunset to sunrise (or, in Alaska, during the period a prominent unlighted object cannot be seen from a distance of 3 statute miles or the sun is more than 6 degrees below the horizon)— (1) Operate an aircraft unless it has lighted position lights;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At night you see another aeroplane ahead with its red light on the left and its green light on the right. What does this tell you?
notes.back: B) It is flying in the same direction as you; keep clear
notes.explanation: Care must still be taken to maintain clearance from it.
notes.choices:
A) It could be on a collision course with you
B) It is flying in the same direction as you; keep clear
C) It is crossing from right to left
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the case when red is on the right and green on the left. C: seeing both wingtip lights with red on the left means it is heading the same way.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airplane Equipment and Lighting”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: If both a red and green light of another aircraft are observed, and the red light is on the left and the green to the right, the airplane is flying the same direction. Care must be taken to maintain clearance.

notes.front: At night you see another aeroplane with its green light on your left and its red light on your right. What might that mean?
notes.back: C) It could be on a collision course with you
notes.explanation: The handbook's wording is 'could be': treat it as a possible collision course.
notes.choices:
A) It is flying the same direction as you
B) It is climbing away from you
C) It could be on a collision course with you
notes.choicesExplained: A: same direction shows red on the left and green on the right. B: the lights show direction of movement, not climb.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Airplane Equipment and Lighting”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: If red were on the right and green to the left, the airplane could be on a collision course.

notes.front: Lining up for a night takeoff, how bright should you set the flight deck lights?
notes.back: At the minimum that still lets you read the instruments and switches without hindering outside vision.
notes.explanation: Dimming the lights also removes reflections on the windshield and windows.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Takeoff and Climb”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: The pilot should adjust the flight deck lights to a minimum brightness that will allow for reading the instruments and switches but not hinder outside vision. Dimming the lights also eliminates reflections on the windshield and windows.

notes.front: Your night cross-country course runs near the edge of your sectional chart. What else should you carry, and why?
notes.back: The adjacent chart, to identify city and town lights that can be seen at surprising distances.
notes.explanation: Without it, those landmarks may go unidentified and confusion could result.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Pilot Equipment”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Aeronautical charts are essential for night cross-country flight and, if the intended course is near the edge of the chart, the adjacent chart should also be available. The lights of cities and towns can be seen at surprising distances at night, and if this adjacent chart is not available to identify those landmarks, confusion could result.

notes.front: On a night VFR flight, the ground lights ahead start to show a halo or glow. What does this indicate?
notes.back: Ground fog: continuing in that direction calls for caution.
notes.explanation: The first sign of restricted visibility is usually the gradual disappearance of ground lights.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Orientation and Navigation”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Usually, the first indication of flying into restricted visibility conditions is the gradual disappearance of lights on the ground. If the lights begin to appear surrounded by a halo or glow, further flight in the same direction calls for caution. Such a halo or glow around lights on the ground is indicative of ground fog.

notes.front: Approaching an unfamiliar airport at night through a maze of city lights, what should you normally fly towards?
notes.back: The rotating beacon, until the lights outlining the runway can be distinguished.
notes.explanation: To fly a pattern of the right size and direction, the threshold and runway-edge lights must be positively identified.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Approaches and Landings”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: A pilot should normally fly toward the rotating beacon until the lights outlining the runway are distinguishable. To fly a traffic pattern of proper size and direction, the runway threshold and runway-edge lights need to be positively identified.

notes.front: Your engine fails at night over nearby terrain you know is suitable for a forced landing. Where should you plan to land?
notes.back: On an unlighted portion of the area.
notes.explanation: This advice applies when the nearby terrain is known and suitable for a forced landing.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Night Emergencies”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: If the condition of the nearby terrain is known and is suitable for a forced landing, turn towards an unlighted portion of the area and plan an emergency forced landing to an unlighted portion.

notes.front: In a night forced landing, your landing lights do not work and you have no outside visual references. How do you hold the aeroplane?
notes.back: In a level-landing attitude until the ground is contacted.
notes.explanation: With lights, the landing is made in the normal landing attitude at the slowest possible airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Night Emergencies”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: The landing should be completed in the normal landing attitude at the slowest possible airspeed. If the landing lights are unusable and outside visual references are not available, the airplane should be held in level-landing attitude until the ground is contacted.

notes.front: On a dark night you approach a runway across a lake, with no other lights around it. What should you use to fly the approach?
notes.back: B) An electronic glide slope or VASI if available; otherwise the flight instruments
notes.explanation: Where navigation aids are unavailable, the flight instruments help keep orientation and a normal approach.
notes.choices:
A) Your sense of the runway's shape through the windscreen
B) An electronic glide slope or VASI if available; otherwise the flight instruments
C) A low, flat approach to keep the lights in view
notes.choicesExplained: A: over featureless terrain the runway can seem to slope, so its picture misleads. C: the worst case of this illusion is landing short.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Featureless Terrain Illusion”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If an electronic glide slope or visual approach slope indicator (VASI) is available, it should be used. If navigation aids (NAVAIDs) are unavailable, the flight instruments assist in maintaining orientation and a normal approach.

notes.front: At night you spot a long straight line of evenly spaced lights ahead where you expect the runway. What should you suspect?
notes.back: C) It may be a road or train, not the runway
notes.explanation: Bright runway lighting with few lights around it is another ground lighting illusion, making the runway seem closer.
notes.choices:
A) It must be the runway, since it is straight
B) It is the approach lighting system
C) It may be a road or train, not the runway
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: road and train lights along a straight path can be mistaken for runway and approach lights.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Ground Lighting Illusions”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Lights along a straight path, such as a road or lights on moving trains, can be mistaken for runway and approach lights. Bright runway and approach lighting systems, especially where few lights illuminate the surrounding terrain, may create the illusion of less distance to the runway.

notes.front: Taking off at night on a runway with no centreline lighting, how do you find the centre?
notes.back: From the painted centreline and the distance to the runway edge lights on each side.
notes.explanation: The heading indicator should also match the known runway direction.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Takeoff and Climb”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: If the runway does not have centerline lighting, the painted centerline and the distance from the runway edge lights on each side indicate the center. The heading indicator should be noted and correspond or set to the known runway direction.

notes.front: Just after a night takeoff with few visual references ahead, the aeroplane starts to veer left. What error has an inexperienced pilot likely made?
notes.back: Relaxing right rudder pressure after takeoff.
notes.explanation: The climb is set using both outside lights and the flight instruments.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 11 “Night Operations”, “Takeoff and Climb”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: As the airspeed reaches the normal lift-off speed, the pilot adjusts the pitch attitude to establish a normal climb by referring to both outside visual references, such as lights, and to the flight instruments. [Figure 11-5] Without visual references ahead, inexperienced pilots may relax right rudder pressure after takeoff and veer off to the left.
